transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-07
Start: 09:23 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Alex Garcia (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Dr. Maya Patel (Cypress Head of Research), Evan Cole (IT Security), Sofia Reyes (Compliance), Liam Chen (Platform)

Summary: discovery focused on HIPAA handling for research PHI-like datasets, routing options between Hosted/Dedicated/Private, log redaction and retention constraints, key management, and a POC path. Customer emphasized auditability, minimal cross-region egress, and on-prem eligibility for sensitive cohorts.

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining — Alex from Redwood, with Priya on the call. Can we do quick intros please?
[00:18] Dr. Maya: Sure, I'm Maya Patel, Head of Research at Cypress Biotech. We run clinical-scale NLP on study notes, some PHI, Some PII, you know the drill.
[00:28] Evan: Evan Cole, I run IT Security. I'm here to make sure whatever we do meets HIPAA and our internal data handling policies.
[00:34] Sofia: Sofia Reyes, Compliance. I'll be validating the controls and evidence for audits.
[00:39] Priya: Great, thanks. Quick context from Redwood: we serve hosted, dedicated, and private deployments. Hosted is fastest but you know tenure around residency, dedicated is reserved capacity in our cloud with stronger isolation, private is VPC or on-prem where control plane can be customer-managed.
[01:05] Liam: Quick question, when you say private — is that fully on-prem or just VPC in our cloud?
[01:11] Alex: Both. We offer a private package that can be deployed into a customer VPC, and we also have an on-prem appliance for air-gapped sites. The control plane options vary with the package.
[01:22] Dr. Maya: Important — some of our datasets cannot leave US region boundaries. Others are more sensitive and prefer on-prem. We're trying to map which workloads could be hosted vs dedicated vs fully private.
[01:35] Priya: That's a common split. For HIPAA, we usually recommend dedicated or private depending on audit requirements. Hosted can be HIPAA-compatible but often requires tighter contractual SLAs and careful data flow configs.
[01:47] Evan: On the logging side — we need audit logs for all inference requests that touch PHI, but logs themselves must be redacted for PHI and stored for seven years, encrypted at rest, and with restricted access. Can Redwood support log redaction at the ingest layer?
[02:05] Priya: Short answer: yes. We have configurable redaction hooks that can scrub PII/PHI before persisting logs. Implementation depends on where you want that logic — at the client side, at our edge router, or inside the runtime.
[02:20] Sofia: We also need evidence for the redaction logic — like hashes of deleted items, not the raw values. Is there a way to keep a tamper-evident trail?
[02:29] Alex: We can surface audit artifacts: k/v hash manifests and signed attestations of redaction events. We'll need to check specifics for legal sufficiency, but we can definitely produce cryptographic hashes and sequencing.
[02:44] Dr. Maya: When you say hashes, do you mean the full prompt text is hashed? We need to ensure re-identification risk is minimized even in hashed form.
[02:54] Priya: Good call. We typically recommend one-way salted hashes with a customer-controlled salt (stored in KMS) and not storing raw context. Also can avoid hashing long free-text — instead hash token identifiers or metadata.
[03:10] Liam: Speaking of KMS — can you integrate with our HSM or eks KMS?
[03:15] Alex: We integrate with common cloud KMS providers and can support customer-managed keys in dedicated/private. For on-prem HSM we have an integration playbook but it'll be part of the private deployment scoping.
[03:28] Evan: Another constraint — no cross-account logging access. The Security team must own the logs and only a narrow ops group should be able to decrypt.
[03:35] Priya: That's inline with our RBAC model — per-tenant roles and audit-imposed ACLs. For private deployments the key ownership stays with you. For dedicated we can set a customer-managed key as well.
[03:48] [00:04:18] Dr. Maya: How does routing work in multi-region? For example, if a researcher in EU needs to run analysis on de-identified data derived in US, is data allowed to transit EU?
[04:30] Priya: Within Redwood there's routing policies: you can pin models to region, enforce region-lock for requests, or set fallbacks. For research-derived de-identified datasets, you'd probably want region locks and explicit routing to US-only nodes.
[04:46] Alex: Also note we can do model variants — run smaller quantized model in EU that doesn't have access to PHI buckets, but again depends on your risk tolerance.
[04:58] Evan: Let's get concrete: for PHI workloads we need all inference execution to run in a US-region only, logs kept in a US KMS, and no backups leaving region.
[05:09] Alex: Understood. We can set tenancy and storage region constraints at project scope. Would you like us to produce a mapping doc for your typical workloads?
[05:18] Dr. Maya: Yes, a mapping would help. We'll tag datasets by sensitivity: public research, de-identified research, and PHI-containing clinical notes.
[05:27] Sofia: On retention — seven years for logs, some internal clinical notes need three years unless associated with a trial which is longer. Can retention be policy-driven per dataset?
[05:37] Priya: Yes, retention is policy-driven. We can configure retention per route/model or per project label. We also support legal hold flags to prevent deletion during investigations.
[05:48] [00:06:30] Liam: For the POC, what footprint do you need? We'll probably start with a small dataset and synthetic PHI to validate. Any constraints on sample sizes?
[06:03] Priya: For latency/throughput benchmarks we prefer representative workloads — so similar sequence lengths and concurrency. For privacy validation, synthetic PHI is fine. We usually run a 1-2 week POC with a dedicated slot or private deployment depending on your needs.
[06:16] Dr. Maya: We have bench-marking questions: token-level auditing, KV cache behavior (we call it KV cache but sometimes docs say KV cash), and whether prefix caching could leak prior session context.
[06:30] Alex: Good pickup — prefix/KV cache is an optimization that stores key-value states for active sessions. For sensitive workloads we can disable KV cache for a route or ensure cache is per-tenant with immediate eviction and not persisted to disk.
[06:45] Evan: You mentioned earlier the ability to scrub before persist. We need to see a sample pipeline — i.e., request flow: client -> edge -> redaction -> runtime -> response and then logging. Can you share a diagram?
[06:56] Alex: We'll include a diagram in the follow-up packet — showing ingress redaction, policy engine, routing, and audit log generation with KMS-wrapped signatures.
[07:06] [00:07:30] Sophia/Sofia: typo — I mean Sofia. Sorry.
[07:10] Priya: No worries. A note on contractual terms: hosted HIPAA requires BAA language and specific data processing addenda. Dedicated/private deployments generally have easier contract negotiables for residency.
[07:24] Sofia: For evidence — besides logs, auditors want configuration snapshots, user access lists, and signing keys rotation history. Can Redwood export configuration snapshots?
[07:34] Priya: Yes, configuration snapshots and a change log that includes the actor, timestamp, and diff are available. That can be bundled for audits.
[07:45] [00:08:15] Dr. Maya: On de-identification — we use a combination of rule-based and ML techniques. If Redwood performs any automatic PII masking, we need to validate false positive/negative rates. Is there a way to run validation tests?
[08:00] Priya: You can run test suites during POC. We'll provide tooling to inject labeled examples and compare outcomes, and tune the redaction rules together.
[08:12] Liam: Network egress is a blocker for us. Some of our sites sit behind strict outbound rules. Will Redwood provide NAT or peering options for private deployments?
[08:22] Alex: For private in-VPC we can peer or establish direct connect. On-prem has a connector that talks outbound to an orchestrator only if you opt in. We'll itemize connectivity options in the doc.
[08:34] Evan: Monitoring — we need SIEM integration and S3-like immutable log dumps. Can you stream audit logs to our Splunk/Graylog?
[08:43] Priya: Yes, streaming to your SIEM over TLS with client certs is supported. Immutable append-only log storage can be sent to a customer-owned bucket.
[08:52] [00:09:30] Dr. Maya: A concern — model hallucination producing PHI-like artifacts. For example a model invents a patient name. Who owns the risk?
[09:01] Alex: That's a great question. Operationally you control input routing and redaction; however the model output is probabilistic. We recommend guardrails: output filters, reranking models, and human-in-the-loop checks for critical flows. Contractually, responsibility clauses depend on configuration and whether Redwood or customer performs post-processing. We'll flag this for legal.
[09:24] Sofia: We'll need to involve legal to go over liability and indemnification.
[09:28] Alex: Totally — we'll slot legal in subsequent meetings.
[09:32] [00:10:00] Priya: Quick technical deep dive — if you run Dedicated, you get a reserved GPU pool in a specific region, isolated network namespaces, and the ability to enforce customer KMS keys. Private on-prem lets you control all persistence and the control plane talkback can be restricted.
[10:15] Liam: For the reserved pool, can we pin instance types? We prefer A100 vs other accelerators for certain models.
[10:21] Priya: Yes, reserved pools can be provisioned with specific hardware families. We'll need capacity lead time.
[10:28] Evan: About encryption — does Redwood do envelope encryption and rotate data keys?
[10:33] Alex: Envelope encryption is standard; data keys are wrapped with KMS and rotations can be orchestrated. For private you manage the root key.
[10:40] [00:11:00] Dr. Maya: How do you handle backups for model artifacts? We have some internal IP in custom model checkpoints.
[11:06] Priya: Model artifacts in private are stored in your storage with optional encryption. For dedicated we isolate model artifacts per account and can accept customer-supplied model packages. Backups are configurable and can be restricted to specific retention.
[11:20] Dr. Maya: Do you do any telemetry or product analytics that might leak model usage?
[11:26] Alex: We collect telemetry for performance, but for dedicated/private we can limit telemetry to aggregate metrics and disable payload telemetry.
[11:34] [00:12:00] Evan: For the POC success criteria: we'll need (1) evidence of redaction effectiveness, (2) audit log proofs with hashed artifacts, (3) latency under X for our sample workload, (4) SIEM integration working. Is that reasonable?
[12:12] Priya: Yes, and add (5) region-lock enforcement test. We'll draft a POC checklist.
[12:20] [00:12:30] Sofia: Any certifications you already have? SOC 2 Type II was mentioned earlier in pre-call notes. HIPAA itself isn't a certification, but do you have SOC2 + penetration test reports?
[12:41] Alex: We have SOC 2 Type II and yearly pen tests. We'll share summary reports and redacted evidence. For HIPAA we provide a BAA and technical controls to meet the rule.
[12:55] Dr. Maya: Does Redwood support consent flags tied to a patient record that prevent processing?
[13:02] Priya: You can pass metadata flags per request and apply policy in the router to block or route to a private path.
[13:12] [00:13:00] Liam: About cost — private on-prem obviously shifts infra cost to us. Dedicated has a monthly reservation. Any rough numbers you can ballpark before formal quote?
[13:23] Alex: We'll avoid hard numbers on the call. Ballpark: dedicated baseline starts with reserved node blocks; private depends on infra specs. We'll follow up with pricing ranges and a cost model comparing hosted vs dedicated vs private for your throughput profile.
[13:40] Priya: We also include Optimize recommendations to suggest quantization/ batching to reduce per token spend without sacrificing your accuracy.
[13:52] [00:14:00] Dr. Maya: Is there a way to run a canary so only a subset of traffic hits Redwood while the rest stays on our current in-house inference?
[14:07] Alex: Yes — route policies can split traffic by percentage or user-group; we support canary rollouts and rollbacks.
[14:15] Evan: For the canary, we need to ensure traces include an origin flag so we can reconcile logs.
[14:21] Priya: That's supported — add metadata headers and we keep the header in logs (or redact if sensitive).
[14:30] [00:15:00] Dr. Maya: Let's talk timeline. We have an upcoming audit in November. Ideally POC completed by mid-October so legal can consume artifacts by end of October.
[15:10] Alex: That timeline is feasible. POC in late Sep/early Oct, then evidence package for legal in October. We'll confirm slot availability in the next two days.
[15:22] Sofia: On evidence for audit, we'll need chain-of-custody for any redacted items and role-based access proof.
[15:31] Priya: We'll include access logs and chain-of-custody metadata in the audit bundle.
[15:38] [00:16:00] Liam: A technical nit — for requests that accidentally include PHI in prompts, is there a safe mode to automatically decline execution?
[16:12] Priya: Yes, you can configure a policy to block execution if a redaction scoring threshold is exceeded. That will return a blocked response and emit an incident event.
[16:23] Evan: Incident response — can we integrate Redwood alerts into our PagerDuty?
[16:28] Alex: Yes, alert webhooks and incident sink to PagerDuty are supported.
[16:33] [00:17:00] Dr. Maya: For model updates, if Redwood pushes a model change that affects output, can we gate rollout?
[17:08] Priya: Rollouts are controllable — canary, percentage rollout, and automated rollback on quality regressions tied to eval suites. You can pin model versions per project.
[17:19] Dr. Maya: Good. We'll want strict gating for anything that touches PHI.
[17:25] [00:17:30] Alex: Noted. We'll include rollout/guardrail policy examples in the POC runbook.
[17:33] Sofia: Any legal hold support on logs? If there's an investigation we need to freeze deletion.
[17:40] Priya: Yes, legal hold flags prevent purge and we can export the hold artifact.
[17:45] [00:18:00] Liam: A question on service level — what SLA for latency and downtime for dedicated vs private?
[18:02] Alex: Dedicated has an SLA with uptime and tail-latency targets; private SLAs are negotiable and often depend on the infra you manage. We'll share the SLA language for review.
[18:14] Dr. Maya: For observability, can token-level cost be mapped back to a study ID?
[18:22] Priya: Yes, cost attribution can be per-route or per-tag so you can track spend by project/study.
[18:30] [00:19:00] Evan: On-network isolation, will dedicated nodes run in a tenant VPC or shared infra?
[19:05] Priya: Dedicated runs in a single-tenant environment within our cloud tenancy with network isolation; private runs in your VPC or on-prem.
[19:15] [00:19:30] Dr. Maya: Is there an example compliance pack we can hand to auditors showing how you meet the HIPAA technical Safeguards?
[19:40] Alex: Yes — we'll bundle a tech safeguards mapping matrix that maps Redwood controls to HIPAA sections, with evidence pointers.
[19:48] [00:20:00] Sofia: For encryption key rotation, auditors will expect rotation timeline history. Can Redwood show a history for the last 12 months?
[20:09] Priya: Yes, key rotation logs and rotation policy snapshots are available in the audit bundle.
[20:18] [00:20:30] Liam: Let's get into POC detail — what endpoints, sample sizes, and benchmarks will you need?
[20:38] Priya: We'll ask for sample payloads: typical prompt sizes, concurrency targets, and examples of sensitive fields. Also a list of evaluation prompts for redaction accuracy.
[20:49] Dr. Maya: We'll prepare a de-identified and a synthetic PHI set. For latency we'll target 95th percentile under 300ms for small prompts.
[20:59] Alex: Got it. We'll include perf targets in the POC runbook.
[21:05] [00:21:00] Evan: For logging retention and legal jurisdiction, we need all logs stored in US-central. Can you guarantee no DR backups in another region?
[21:18] Priya: We can configure geo-replication options per-project; for strict residency we can turn off cross-region replication and keep backups in the region. We'll note that some managed services have soft limits for regional failover — we'll document the options.
[21:33] [00:21:30] Dr. Maya: Are there any known limitations with large batch inference and retention?
[21:44] Priya: Not specifically. We will profile throughput and advise batch sizes that don't increase leakage risk.
[21:51] [00:22:00] Alex: Quick recap — action items and next steps: Alex to share whitepaper and SOC2 artifacts, Priya to draft POC runbook, Cypress to send dataset tags and retention rules. We'll propose POC dates.
[22:12] Dr. Maya: Sounds good. Anything else?
[22:16] Sofia: One last ask — can Redwood provide a short reference call with a healthcare customer who did HIPAA POC?
[22:25] Alex: We can arrange a reference; will check with customers and share availability.
[22:31] [00:22:45] Evan: Thanks. If you can send the security pack and a proposed POC schedule that'd be great.
[22:39] Alex: Yes — we'll send by 2026-09-10.
[22:44] [00:23:00] Priya: Closing — we'll align on POC scope in the doc and follow up with legal and engineering hooks.
[23:00] Dr. Maya: Appreciate it.
[23:04] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and schedule.

End of transcript (approx 23 minutes captured; meeting continued with deeper technical scoping and a short screen-share that had poor audio transcription — remainder summarized in action items).

Notes on transcription quality: parts of the screen-share (model demo and network diagram) didn't transcribe cleanly; some technical terms mistranscribed (e.g., "KV cache" as "K-V cash").
